Treat it like a vendor. Ask who controls the thermostat, and whether there's a coat check. Outdoors, even briefly? Heaters, blankets, hot drinks. Two: light. Here's the part people skip: the clock. People say winter sunsets are around five. On December twenty-first, they're not. New York, four thirty-two. Chicago, four twenty-three. Seattle, four twenty. Los Angeles, four forty-eight. Same city, different date? New York's sunset is five twenty-eight on February thirteenth. Check the sunset for your date and city. Then visit the venue at that hour. Warm the room with candles, string lights and a soft glow. And ask your photographer about low-light work. Three: a plan B you've actually seen. Walk the indoor backup yourself, even if they say it never snows. Price the tents and heaters, because bad weather raises costs. Decide by about five months out. And decide how you'll tell guests if plans change. Save this for your venue walk-through. Four: the calendar, if you're near a holiday. One guide suggests save-the-dates ten to twelve months ahead. Add hotel and travel details to the invitation, because winter weather disrupts trips. Five: what the season grows and cooks. Planners' winter lists name amaryllis, anemones, ranunculus and hellebores, plus greenery. Menu ideas lean warm: soups, braises, a hot-chocolate bar. None of this means you're behind.
